title: Desk Lamp Story Problem Card Pack
audience: Families, co-op groups, tutors, and adult-led writing tables for writers ages 7-11.
sessionLength: 16 printable problem cards plus adult guide tools, problem routines, take-home problem slips, and optional share prompts
safetyNote: No scary harm, no bullying, no romance, no weapons, no branded characters, no real child profiles.

cover.headline: Desk Lamp Story Problem Card Pack
cover.subhead: Sixteen paper cards help writers shape fictional story problems with problem spots, character needs, place pressure, object trouble, questions, first tries, and revision prompts.

beforeSession: Print the problem cards, blank slips, and adult guide before the adult-led paper session.
Use a drawn desk lamp or pretend paper lamp as the shared story prop.
Keep every prompt fictional, broad, offline, and printable from start to finish.
Choose a small stack so each writer works with one gentle obstacle at a time.
Remind writers that a first try can be changed when the problem becomes clearer.
deskLampProblemSetup: Place the drawn desk lamp at the center of the paper set with four beam labels: clue, want, mismatch, first try.
Let the adult read the card and point to the beam label that starts the problem.
Ask writers to invent one made-up character, one missing clue, and one small story problem.
Use blank slips for extra tries so crossed-out ideas can stay low-pressure.
Keep the lamp idea broad: a glow, shade, pull cord, switch, base, or label can all become paper clues.
problemCoaching: Ask what feels missing, mixed up, or not yet clear in the made-up story.
Keep the obstacle small enough for one character choice and one first try.
If the problem gets too large, shrink it to one clue under the lamp glow.
Ask which detail changes after the first try so the next sentence has a purpose.
Use gentle revision by swapping one vague word for a clearer invented clue.
privacyAndSafetyNotes: Use invented names, broad story labels, and pretend places only.
Keep the activity paper-only, offline, and adult-led.
Do not collect facts about actual writers, families, or daily life.
If a detail sounds personal, replace it with a made-up lamp label or story object.
Sharing stays optional and limited to one fictional word, sketch, or line.
familyHandoff: Pass along one chosen paper slip and one blank slip for another fictional problem.
Tell family adults to ask about the made-up obstacle, not actual life details.
Invite praise for one clear clue, one first try, or one revised problem word.
Keep the carry-along activity adult-led, offline, and paper-only.
Ask family adults to leave narrow personal facts off the paper and keep the story invented.
reset: Collect unused cards, blank slips, and the drawn desk lamp prop.
Recycle scratch paper that includes narrow real-world facts.
Save only fictional examples that can model gentle obstacles later.
Restock the pack with fresh blank slips before the next paper session.

problemRoutines.name: Beam Label Pick
problemRoutines.bestFor: Writers who need a simple way to name the small story problem.
steps: The adult points to one lamp beam label: clue, want, mismatch, or first try.
The writer chooses one invented object under that beam.
The adult asks what small problem appears because the object is missing, mixed up, or unclear.
The writer writes one sentence that names the gentle obstacle.

problemRoutines.name: Missing Clue Glow
problemRoutines.bestFor: Writers who can start once one clue is absent or hidden.
steps: The adult draws a glow circle on a blank slip.
The writer names the invented clue that should be inside the glow.
The adult asks why the character needs that clue before moving on.
The writer adds one first try that brings the clue closer.

problemRoutines.name: Switch Mismatch
problemRoutines.bestFor: Turning a mismatch into a clear fictional problem.
steps: The adult sketches an on-off switch on paper.
The writer invents what changes when the switch moves.
The adult asks what no longer matches after the switch change.
The writer writes the mismatch as a small story problem.

problemRoutines.name: Shade the Too-Big Problem
problemRoutines.bestFor: Shrinking a large idea into one writable obstacle.
steps: The adult draws a lamp shade over the largest part of the problem idea.
The writer chooses only one visible clue to keep.
The adult asks what the character can try first with that clue.
The writer rewrites the problem as one clear sentence.

problemRoutines.name: Question Under the Lamp
problemRoutines.bestFor: Writers who need the problem to become a question before drafting.
steps: The adult places a blank question slip under the drawn desk lamp.
The writer names one character want and one missing clue.
The adult helps turn those two pieces into a gentle question.
The writer answers the question with a first try, not the final fix.

problemRoutines.name: First Try, Better Try
problemRoutines.bestFor: Showing that a problem can grow clearer after one attempt.
steps: The adult reads the problem card and asks for one first try.
The writer writes the try even if it is not enough yet.
The adult asks what clue the try reveals.
The writer revises the problem using the new clue.
